requirements: The core contributions of the paper 'BAPS: A Fine-Grained Low-Precision Scheme for Softmax in Attention via Block-Aware Precision reScaling' have been reproduced.

sub_tasks.requirements: The software environment, HiF8 simulation infrastructure, and FP8 format support required to run the BAPS workflow are correctly established.
A Python environment with the required dependencies for running Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, Llama-3.1-8B, and Wan-2.2 inference with a custom low-precision attention path is set up.
Code has been implemented that pins Python, PyTorch (with CUDA), and Hugging Face transformers versions capable of loading Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and Llama-3.1-8B in BF16 for inference.
Code has been implemented that installs the diffusers/Wan-2.2 pipeline dependencies (including video I/O libraries) required for text-to-video generation experiments.

Code has been implemented that installs benchmark harnesses / dataset loaders for RULER (CWE), MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, and MATH-500 so the evaluation pipeline can be launched against the wrapped low-precision attention module.

Code has been implemented that fixes a single global random seed (torch, numpy, python-random, and CUDA generators) across all Default / Exp2 HiF8 / E2E HiF8 configurations so ablation runs are directly comparable, as stated in Section 4.1.
The HiF8 numerical format and its FP16-based simulation of powers-of-two (Algorithm 2) are implemented as reusable primitives.

Code has been implemented providing a HiF8 quantize/dequantize routine that takes FP16 (or FP32) inputs, casts them to the HiF8 dynamic exponent-mantissa encoding described by Luo et al. (2024), and returns FP16 tensors that carry only bits representable in HiF8.
The HiF8 quantizer, when applied to a value already representable in HiF8, is idempotent: quantize(quantize(x)) equals quantize(x) bit-for-bit in the FP16 storage.

Code has been implemented for the `exp2_hif8` primitive that follows Algorithm 2 exactly: FP16 input -> cast to HiF8 -> cast back to FP16 -> exp2 in FP16 -> cast to HiF8 -> cast back to FP16 as the returned value.

The `exp2_hif8` primitive, when called on integer inputs in [-20, 0], returns values whose relative error vs FP32 exp2 is bounded by the HiF8 output-format resolution (i.e., no accumulated FP16 rounding beyond a single HiF8 round-trip on the output).
Supporting FP8 formats (E4M3, E5M2, and the mixed E4M3xE5M2 configuration) are implemented so that the FP8-format ablation in Table 1 can be run alongside HiF8.

Code has been implemented providing E4M3 and E5M2 quantize/dequantize routines (4/3 and 5/2 exponent/mantissa bit-width, respecting each format's finite/inf/NaN conventions) usable interchangeably with the HiF8 primitive.

Code has been implemented for an `exp2_fp8` primitive parameterized by (input_format, output_format) so that Exp2 E4M3, Exp2 E5M2, Exp2 E4M3xE5M2, and Exp2 HiF8 can all be instantiated from the same code path used in Algorithm 2.

A configuration mechanism selects among the three evaluated attention setups (Default, Exp2 HiF8, E2E HiF8) and the additional Table 1 ablations, and wires the chosen setup into the model's attention module.

Code has been implemented that exposes a single configuration flag/enum selecting one of {Default, Exp2 E4M3, Exp2 E5M2, Exp2 E4M3xE5M2, Exp2 HiF8, E2E HiF8, Naive E2E} and dispatches to the corresponding attention kernel variant.

In the Default configuration, inputs Q/K/V are stored in BF16 and every operation inside softmax (subtraction of row-max, exponentiation, denominator accumulation, normalization) is executed in FP32, matching the Section 4.1 Default definition.
In the Exp2 HiF8 configuration, the attention path is identical to Default except that every power-of-two exponentiation inside softmax is routed through the HiF8 `exp2_hif8` primitive.

The E2E HiF8 configuration wires Algorithm 1 into the attention module: the first tile of each input sequence is placed in B0, all remaining tiles in B1, and the restart threshold defaults to lambda = 1 unless overridden.

Code has been implemented for the Naive E2E baseline that directly casts the score matrix S to HiF8 before subtracting the row maximum (i.e., no offloaded subtraction, no restart), so it can be compared against E2E HiF8 in Table 1.
The Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, Llama-3.1-8B, and Wan-2.2 models along with the RULER (CWE), MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, MATH-500 benchmarks and the 8 T2V prompts are available for evaluation.
Language models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and Llama-3.1-8B) are acquired and loadable for inference.
Code has been implemented to download and load the Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 model checkpoint (as referenced in Section 4.2) in BF16 precision for the query/key/value tensors.
Code has been implemented to download and load the Llama-3.1-8B model checkpoint in BF16 precision, matching the setup described in Section 4.2.
The loaded language models can perform single-shot inference on natural-language prompts and return generated tokens, as required for MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, and MATH-500 evaluations.
The Wan-2.2 multi-modal text-to-video model is acquired and set up for T2V generation.
Code has been implemented to download and load the Wan-2.2 multi-modal model checkpoint referenced in Section 4.3 for text-to-video generation.
The Wan-2.2 pipeline supports the T2V generation configuration used in the paper, including the single-frame 40-sampling-step run (Section 4.3) and full multi-frame generation across the 8 prompts.
The RULER CWE benchmark data is prepared for evaluating long-context accuracy at multiple sequence lengths.
Code has been implemented to generate or download the RULER Common Word Extraction (CWE) subtask samples at input sequence lengths of 32K, 64K, and 96K tokens.
Each CWE sequence length yields exactly 100 randomly generated test samples, matching the dataset composition described in Section 4.2.
Code has been implemented to score CWE outputs (percentage accuracy of extracted common words) so that CWE accuracy per sequence length can be computed for each configuration.
The language-reasoning benchmarks MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, and MATH-500 are available and integrated for single-shot evaluation.

Code has been implemented to download and load the MMLU-Pro benchmark, including access to all 14 sub-tasks (Computer Science, Math, Chemistry, Engineering, Law, Biology, Health, Physics, Business, Philosophy, Economics, Other, Psychology, History) as listed in Tables 5-6.
Code has been implemented to download and load the GPQA-Diamond benchmark for single-shot evaluation.
Code has been implemented to download and load the MATH-500 dataset, including problem difficulty-level labels (levels 1-5) as referenced in Tables 7-8.
Evaluation harness runs each benchmark with a single shot per test sample (matching Section 4.2) and computes percentage accuracy per sub-task/level and overall.
The 8 text-to-video prompts used for Wan-2.2 evaluation are available verbatim as inputs.

Code or data has been provided containing the exact 8 T2V prompts shown in Figures 5-12 (Tokyo woman, wooly mammoths, spaceman trailer, Big Sur drone, fluffy monster with candle, papercraft coral reef, Victoria crowned pigeon, pirate ships in coffee cup).

The T2V generation pipeline uses a fixed random seed shared across Default, Exp2 HiF8, and E2E HiF8 configurations so that videos generated from each prompt are directly comparable, as stated in Section 4.1.
The 8-bit exponentiation module for computing P from S - rowfill(m), including support for E4M3, E5M2, mixed E4M3xE5M2, and HiF8 formats, is implemented as described in Section 3.1.
The core exponentiation kernel that computes P^(j)_i = 2^(S^(j)_i - rowfill(m^(j)_i)) is implemented with configurable input and output FP8 numerical formats.
Code has been implemented that computes 2^(S - rowfill(m)) element-wise given a tile of scores S and a per-row maximum vector m, where m is broadcast across the row via a rowfill operation.
Code has been implemented that exposes a configurable option to select the input FP8 format (used to represent S - rowfill(m) prior to exponentiation) from {E4M3, E5M2, HiF8}.

Code has been implemented that exposes a configurable option to select the output FP8 format (used to represent P = 2^(S - rowfill(m))) from {E4M3, E5M2, HiF8}, allowing independent choice of input vs. output precision to support the mixed E4M3xE5M2 configuration.

When invoked with input format = E4M3 and output format = E5M2, the exponentiation kernel casts the subtraction result to E4M3, computes powers of two, and casts the result to E5M2, matching the Exp2 E4M3xE5M2 configuration described in Section 3.1.
FP8 numeric format casts (E4M3, E5M2) required by the exponentiation module are implemented with correct saturation, rounding, and dynamic-range behavior.
Code has been implemented that casts FP32/FP16 values to E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) with correct handling of saturation and rounding to nearest.
Code has been implemented that casts FP32/FP16 values to E5M2 (5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa bits) with correct handling of saturation and rounding.
The E4M3 cast, when applied to values in [0, 2^-9), produces zero or the smallest denormal representable, reflecting E4M3's limited resolution in this range as discussed in Section 3.1.
The E5M2 cast retains representable resolution for values in [0, 2^-9), demonstrating the wider dynamic range that motivates its use for outputs P^(j)_i.
The HiF8-based exponentiation path used by the default Exp2 HiF8 configuration is implemented following Algorithm 2 of Appendix A.1.

Code has been implemented that simulates HiF8 exponentiation by (i) truncating the FP16 input to HiF8, (ii) restoring back to FP16, (iii) computing exp2 in FP16, (iv) truncating the result to HiF8, and (v) restoring back to FP16, matching Algorithm 2.
The HiF8 cast function is implemented as a truncation from FP16 to HiF8 followed by a lossless expansion back to FP16, matching the simulated behavior described in Appendix A.1.
The HiF8 exponentiation path is invoked as the exponentiation module inside the Exp2 HiF8 configuration for both Section 3.1 exponentiation of P and downstream softmax computation.
The exponentiation module is integrated into the attention/softmax pipeline as the operation that produces P from the (S - rowfill(m)) tile.

Within the online-softmax tile update, the module receives (S^(j)_i - rowfill(m^(j)_i)) after the per-row maximum subtraction and returns P^(j)_i in the configured 8-bit output format for consumption by the subsequent P·V matmul.

Because (S - rowfill(m)) is predominantly non-positive, the module produces outputs P ∈ [0, 1] for well-formed inputs; the code does not depend on any part of the output range above 1 for correctness of the exponentiation path.

Behavioral verification confirms that the mixed E4M3xE5M2 configuration and the HiF8 configuration approximate the FP32 baseline distribution of 2^(S - rowfill(m)) more closely than the pure E4M3 or pure E5M2 configurations, consistent with the CDFs in Figure 1b.

A comparison test measures the discrepancy (e.g., KS distance or L1 between empirical CDFs) between the FP32 reference distribution of 2^(S - rowfill(m)) and each of {E4M3, E5M2, E4M3xE5M2, HiF8} configurations on scores dumped from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct, and confirms E4M3xE5M2 and HiF8 have smaller discrepancy than pure E4M3 or pure E5M2.

The offloaded subtraction scheme that computes T = (QK^T·log2 e/sqrt(d)) - rowfill(m~) on special-purpose accelerators and transfers 8-bit T is implemented, including the approximate maximum m~ initialization and the restart threshold λ mechanism.
The tile partitioning into B0 (critical tiles for approximate maximum initialization) and B1 (remaining tiles using offloaded subtraction) is implemented.

Code has been implemented that partitions the tiles along the key sequence into two sets B0 and B1, where B0 contains critical tiles processed first (by default the first tile of each input sequence) and B1 contains the remaining tiles.

Code has been implemented such that tiles in B0 are computed with the high-precision path that produces S^(j)_i in high precision and updates m^(j)_i = max(m^(j-1)_i, ceil(rowmax(S^(j)_i))) before entering the offloaded low-precision path used for B1.
The approximate row-wise maximum m~^(j)_i initialization and its usage in the offloaded subtraction are implemented.
Code has been implemented that initializes the approximate row-wise maximum m~^(j)_i as m^(j-1)_i (the maximum from the previous iteration) for tiles j in B1, as specified in Algorithm 1 line 11.
Code has been implemented such that when a restart is triggered inside B1, m~^(j)_i is updated to the recomputed m^(j)_i = max(m^(j-1)_i, ceil(rowmax(S^(j)_i))), matching Algorithm 1 lines 15-16.
The fused offloaded subtraction T^(j)_i = Q_i K_j^T · log2(e) / sqrt(d) - rowfill(m~^(j)_i) is implemented on the special-purpose-accelerator side and produces an 8-bit output.

Code has been implemented that fuses the Q_i K_j^T matrix product, the log2(e)/sqrt(d) scaling, and the subtraction of rowfill(m~^(j)_i) into a single computation path that emits T^(j)_i, as in Algorithm 1 line 12.

Code has been implemented that casts / stores T^(j)_i in an 8-bit floating-point representation (HiF8 in the reference implementation) before it is transferred from the special-purpose accelerator to the general-purpose accelerator.

The log2(e)/sqrt(d) scale factor is applied inside the fused MMA-plus-subtract kernel so that T is in base-2 exponent domain, ensuring that the subsequent 2^T operation directly implements exp(S - m~).

For a synthetic Q_i, K_j pair with a known m~, the fused kernel produces T^(j)_i whose 8-bit-decoded values match the mathematical formula (QK^T · log2 e / sqrt(d)) - rowfill(m~) within HiF8 quantization error on every element.
The restart threshold λ mechanism and the associated high-precision recomputation branch are implemented.
Code has been implemented that evaluates the restart condition ceil(rowmax(T^(j)_i)) > λ for tiles in B1, using an integer-valued λ (default λ = 1) exposed as a configurable parameter.

When the restart condition triggers, code recomputes S^(j)_i = Q_i K_j^T · log2 e / sqrt(d) in high precision and then computes T^(j)_i = S^(j)_i - rowfill(m~^(j)_i) with the updated m~^(j)_i, storing/transferring the result in 8-bit as in Algorithm 1 lines 14-17.
When the restart condition does not trigger, code updates m^(j)_i = m^(j-1)_i + max(0, ceil(rowmax(T^(j)_i))) without recomputing S^(j)_i in high precision, matching Algorithm 1 line 19.
Code has been implemented that, upon a restart in B1, also propagates the rescaling of d^(j-1)_i and O~^(j-1)_i so that the online softmax accumulator remains consistent with the updated m^(j)_i.
On a controlled input where all T^(j)_i entries are non-positive, no restart is triggered for any tile in B1 (restart count equals 0), verifying the low-restart branch behaves as specified.

On a controlled input crafted so that ceil(rowmax(T^(j)_i)) exceeds λ for at least one tile, the implementation triggers exactly the expected restart branch for those tiles and produces attention outputs bit-consistent with an all-high-precision reference on the restarted tiles.
Numerical validation that the 8-bit offloading of T combined with the restart mechanism preserves overall model behavior.

The 'Naive E2E' configuration (directly converting scores to HiF8 before subtraction, without the m~ initialization and restart mechanism) reproduces the significant CWE accuracy degradation reported for Qwen3-30B-A3B (e.g., 87.8 at 32K, 54.0 at 64K, 44.0 at 96K), demonstrating that the offloaded-subtraction plus restart mechanism (not raw 8-bit casting) is what preserves accuracy.

With the offloaded 8-bit T scheme enabled (E2E HiF8, λ=1), attention outputs O_i agree with a full-precision Flash-Attention reference within a small tolerance on a synthetic input drawn from the same score distribution family as reported in Figure 1, confirming the offloading path does not introduce systematic bias when restarts are permitted.
The reduction of accumulated error via integer powers of two (ceiling of rowmax when updating m, d, and O) is implemented per Section 3.3.
The integer-exponent update rule for the row-wise maximum m is implemented so that the rescaling factor is always an integer power of two.

Code has been implemented that computes the updated row maximum for tiles in B0 as m^(j)_i = max(m^(j-1)_i, ceil(rowmax(S^(j)_i))), applying an integer ceiling to rowmax before the max reduction, as prescribed in line 5 of Algorithm 1.

Code has been implemented that updates the row maximum for non-restart tiles in B1 as m^(j)_i = m^(j-1)_i + max(0, ceil(rowmax(T^(j)_i))), guaranteeing the offset added is a non-negative integer (line 19 of Algorithm 1).
The ceiling operation applied to rowmax outputs integer-valued exponents (verifiable by a unit test showing all m^(j)_i values are integers throughout the iteration).
The integer power-of-two rescaling is correctly applied when updating the denominator d and un-normalized output O.

Code has been implemented that updates the denominator as d^(j)_i = diag(2^(m^(j-1)_i - m^(j)_i)) * d^(j-1)_i + P^(j)_i * 1, where the exponent (m^(j-1)_i - m^(j)_i) is an integer, matching lines 7 and 22 of Algorithm 1.

Code has been implemented that updates the un-normalized output as O_tilde^(j)_i = diag(2^(m^(j-1)_i - m^(j)_i)) * O_tilde^(j-1)_i + P^(j)_i * V_j using the same integer exponent, matching lines 8 and 23 of Algorithm 1.

The 2^(m^(j-1)_i - m^(j)_i) rescaling factors are computed exactly (e.g., via bit-shift or exact power-of-two representation) so that they introduce no additional floating-point error, distinguishing the implementation from a naive exp2 call on a non-integer exponent.
The exact behavior of integer-exponent rescaling versus non-integer rescaling is verifiable in isolation.

A unit test demonstrates that repeated application of the integer-exponent rescaling factor 2^k (with k an integer) to an accumulator does not accumulate multiplicative error relative to an FP32 reference, whereas applying 2^x with non-integer x does.

Code has been implemented to sweep sequence length (up to at least 500 tokens, matching the range shown in Figure 2) and record the relative accumulated multiplicative error of the online-softmax update against an FP32 ground truth, for both with-ceiling and without-ceiling variants.
The measured accumulated-error behavior of the integer-power-of-two scheme matches the paper's claims.

With integer-exponent ceiling enabled, the relative accumulated multiplicative error stays tightly bounded (i.e., does not grow with sequence length) over sequence lengths up to 500, consistent with the 'w/ ceiling' curve in Figure 2.

Without the integer-exponent ceiling, the relative accumulated multiplicative error visibly grows/oscillates with sequence length and reaches magnitudes on the order of ~6e-3 by sequence length 500, matching the 'w/o ceiling' curve in Figure 2.

Algorithm 1's complete workflow — including partitioning tiles into B0 and B1, restart-triggered high-precision recalculation, and the HiF8-based exponentiation — is implemented end-to-end as the E2E HiF8 configuration.
The workflow partitions key/value tiles into the critical set B0 and the remaining set B1 as specified in Algorithm 1.
Code has been implemented that, for each query tile i, assigns key/value tiles indices to a B0 set and a B1 set before running Algorithm 1's main loop.
Code has been implemented so that, by default configuration for E2E HiF8 experiments, the first tile of each input sequence is placed in B0 and all remaining tiles are placed in B1.

For a given sequence and tile size, the produced B0 and B1 index sets are disjoint, cover every key tile exactly once, and are iterated in the order B0 first, then B1 (matching lines 3-24 of Algorithm 1).
The B0 branch (lines 3-9 of Algorithm 1) computes S, m, P, d, and O in high precision with integer-rounded row maxima.
Code has been implemented that, for each j in B0, computes S_i^{(j)} = Q_i K_j^T · log2(e) / sqrt(d) in high precision (FP32/FP16-level).
Code has been implemented so that, for each j in B0, m_i^{(j)} = max(m_i^{(j-1)}, ceil(rowmax(S_i^{(j)}))) with rowmax rounded up to the nearest integer (as in line 5 of Algorithm 1).
Code has been implemented so that, for each j in B0, P_i^{(j)} = 2^{S_i^{(j)} - rowfill(m_i^{(j)})}, with the power-of-two performed through the HiF8 simulation path.

Code has been implemented so that, for each j in B0, the denominator d_i^{(j)} and un-normalized output O_i^{(j)} are updated using the diag(2^{m_i^{(j-1)} - m_i^{(j)}}) rescaling factor exactly as specified in lines 7-8 of Algorithm 1.
The B1 branch (lines 10-24) computes T in 8-bit using an approximate row maximum and handles the restart condition.
Code has been implemented so that, for each j in B1, the approximate row-wise maximum m_tilde_i^{(j)} is initialized from m_i^{(j-1)} (line 11 of Algorithm 1) prior to computing T.
Code has been implemented so that, for each j in B1, T_i^{(j)} = Q_i K_j^T · log2(e)/sqrt(d) - rowfill(m_tilde_i^{(j)}) is produced in 8-bit (HiF8) precision (line 12 of Algorithm 1).
Code has been implemented so that, for each j in B1, P_i^{(j)} = 2^{T_i^{(j)}} is computed in 8-bit using the HiF8 exponentiation path (line 21 of Algorithm 1).

Code has been implemented so that, for each j in B1, d_i^{(j)} and O_i^{(j)} are updated with diag(2^{m_i^{(j-1)} - m_i^{(j)}}) rescaling followed by accumulation of P_i^{(j)} · 1 and P_i^{(j)} V_j (lines 22-23).
The restart mechanism triggers high-precision recalculation when ceil(rowmax(T)) exceeds the threshold lambda.
Code has been implemented that exposes the restart threshold lambda as a configurable integer parameter and uses lambda = 1 as the default for E2E HiF8 experiments.
Code has been implemented that, for each B1 tile, evaluates the predicate ceil(rowmax(T_i^{(j)})) > lambda to decide whether to trigger a restart (line 13 of Algorithm 1).

Code has been implemented so that, on a restart, S_i^{(j)} is recomputed in high precision, m_i^{(j)} is updated as max(m_i^{(j-1)}, ceil(rowmax(S_i^{(j)}))), m_tilde_i^{(j)} is set to m_i^{(j)}, and T_i^{(j)} = S_i^{(j)} - rowfill(m_tilde_i^{(j)}) is re-cast to 8-bit (lines 14-17).
Code has been implemented so that, when the restart condition is not triggered, m_i^{(j)} = m_i^{(j-1)} + max(0, ceil(rowmax(T_i^{(j)}))) is used (line 19 of Algorithm 1).
The implementation constrains lambda to integer values and rejects or asserts against non-integer thresholds, consistent with the integer-power-of-two rescaling invariant described in Section 4.4.
The final output normalization O_i = diag^{-1}(d_i) O_tilde_i is applied after all tile iterations (line 25 of Algorithm 1).

Code has been implemented that fuses the subtraction of the row maximum into the Q_i K_j^T product on the special-purpose accelerator path (per Section 3.4), so that only 8-bit T is transferred out for B1 tiles rather than the full-precision S.

Code has been implemented that exposes the 'E2E HiF8' configuration as a runnable mode alongside 'Default' and 'Exp2 HiF8', selecting Algorithm 1 with HiF8 exponentiation, tile partitioning, and restart logic all enabled.

Under a deterministic seed and matched inputs, when lambda is set so that every B1 tile triggers a restart, the E2E HiF8 output collapses to the Default (BF16 input, FP32 softmax) numerical behavior up to HiF8 rounding, confirming the restart path is a correct fallback.

The implementation distinguishes E2E HiF8 (post-subtraction 8-bit conversion + restart) from a 'Naive E2E' variant that converts scores directly to HiF8 before subtraction, and this distinction is exercisable as separate runnable configurations.

The comparison of Default, Exp2 E4M3, Exp2 E5M2, Exp2 E4M3xE5M2, Exp2 HiF8, E2E HiF8, and Naive E2E on the CWE subtask of RULER at 32K/64K/96K sequence lengths reproduces the results reported in Table 1.
The CWE evaluation harness for RULER is set up and configured to run at 32K, 64K, and 96K sequence lengths.
Code has been implemented that loads the RULER Common Word Extraction (CWE) subtask configuration and generates evaluation samples at sequence lengths of 32K, 64K, and 96K tokens.
For each sequence length, the CWE test dataset is composed of 100 randomly generated samples using a fixed random seed shared across all configurations.
Code has been implemented that computes CWE accuracy in percentage from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 model outputs on the generated samples.
Each of the seven softmax configurations under comparison is implemented as an attention variant selectable at evaluation time.

Code has been implemented for the Default configuration in which softmax inputs are stored in BF16 and all softmax internal operations execute in FP32 following the standard FlashAttention formulation.

Code has been implemented for the Exp2 E4M3 configuration that casts both the input (S - rowfill(m)) and the output of the power-of-two exponentiation to E4M3 while keeping the rest of the pipeline matching the Default setup.
Code has been implemented for the Exp2 E5M2 configuration that casts both the exponent input and the exponent output to E5M2.
Code has been implemented for the Exp2 E4M3xE5M2 hybrid configuration that uses E4M3 for the exponent input and E5M2 for the exponent output.

Code has been implemented for the Exp2 HiF8 configuration that follows the Default pipeline but performs all power-of-two exponentiation operations using the HiF8 data format (simulated via FP16 through the truncation procedure of Algorithm 2).

Code has been implemented for the E2E HiF8 configuration that follows Algorithm 1 with inputs stored in BF16, extends HiF8 to nearly all softmax operations, assigns the first tile of each sequence to B0 and remaining tiles to B1, and defaults the restart threshold to lambda = 1.

Code has been implemented for the Naive E2E configuration that directly converts the scores S to HiF8 before subtracting the row maximum, without the offloaded subtraction and restart mechanism of Algorithm 1.
The seven configurations behave correctly and are evaluated under a controlled protocol.
All seven configurations are run using the same random seed to ensure consistent randomness across runs, as stated in Section 4.1.
Code has been implemented that dispatches CWE evaluation over all seven configurations x three sequence lengths and writes a results table matching the layout of Table 1.
Reproduce the numerical CWE accuracies of Table 1 for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507.
The Default configuration achieves CWE accuracy of 88.5% at 32K, 64.8% at 64K, and 58.9% at 96K sequence length, matching Table 1.
The Exp2 E4M3 configuration achieves CWE accuracy of 86.1% at 32K, 58.1% at 64K, and 53.0% at 96K, matching Table 1 and showing substantial degradation vs Default at longer lengths.
The Exp2 E5M2 configuration achieves CWE accuracy of 87.8% at 32K, 62.4% at 64K, and 58.5% at 96K, matching Table 1.
The Exp2 E4M3xE5M2 configuration achieves CWE accuracy of 87.5% at 32K, 63.5% at 64K, and 57.4% at 96K, matching Table 1.
The Exp2 HiF8 configuration achieves CWE accuracy of 89.1% at 32K, 63.2% at 64K, and 58.1% at 96K, matching Table 1.
The E2E HiF8 configuration achieves CWE accuracy of 88.0% at 32K, 64.0% at 64K, and 58.3% at 96K, matching Table 1.
The Naive E2E configuration achieves CWE accuracy of 87.8% at 32K, 54.0% at 64K, and 44.0% at 96K, matching Table 1 and demonstrating markedly lower accuracy at longer sequences than E2E HiF8.
At sequence length 64K, Exp2 E4M3xE5M2 and Exp2 HiF8 both outperform Exp2 E4M3 and Exp2 E5M2, consistent with the ordering discussed in Section 4.2.
The Default, Exp2 HiF8, and E2E HiF8 configurations reproduce the overall accuracy on MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, and MATH-500 for Qwen3-30B-A3B and Llama-3.1-8B as reported in Table 2.
Reasoning benchmark harness and evaluation pipeline: infrastructure to run MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, and MATH-500 on the two target models under the three attention configurations.
Code has been implemented to load MMLU-Pro test items and iterate over all 14 subject categories, producing per-item multiple-choice inputs suitable for single-shot evaluation.
Code has been implemented to load the GPQA-Diamond split and construct its multiple-choice prompts.
Code has been implemented to load the MATH-500 problem set (all 500 problems across difficulty levels 1-5) and format each problem for single-shot evaluation.

Evaluation is conducted with a single shot (0-shot / 1 sample per item, no self-consistency majority voting) for each test sample across all three benchmarks, matching the protocol stated in Section 4.2.

Code has been implemented to parse model responses and compute accuracy in percent for MMLU-Pro (extract selected choice), GPQA-Diamond (extract selected choice), and MATH-500 (extract final boxed answer and compare to ground truth).
A fixed random seed is set consistently across the Default, Exp2 HiF8, and E2E HiF8 runs so that all three configurations receive identical inputs and sampling randomness, as required in Section 4.1.
Configuration switching: the three attention configurations (Default, Exp2 HiF8, E2E HiF8) can each be selected for inference on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and Llama-3.1-8B.
The Default configuration performs attention exactly as in Equation (2) with inputs stored in BF16 and all softmax-internal operations in FP32.
The Exp2 HiF8 configuration is identical to Default except that every power-of-two exponentiation in the softmax is executed via the HiF8 simulation path.

The E2E HiF8 configuration implements Algorithm 1 with inputs stored in BF16, HiF8 extended to nearly all softmax-internal operations, the first tile of each sequence assigned to B0 and remaining tiles to B1, and restart threshold lambda = 1 (unless otherwise specified).
A single configuration flag / entry point selects one of {Default, Exp2 HiF8, E2E HiF8} for a full evaluation run without changing any other code path or hyperparameters.
Measured Table 2 accuracies for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 on the three reasoning benchmarks under each configuration.

Code has been implemented that casts FP32 values of S - rowfill(m) to E4M3, E5M2, and HiF8 formats and reads them back to FP32 for CDF plotting, matching the simulation approach described in Algorithm 2.

Code has been implemented that computes 2^(S - rowfill(m)) under each of the five configurations (FP32 baseline; E4M3 in/out; E5M2 in/out; E4M3 in with E5M2 out; HiF8 in/out) so that both the input quantization to exponentiation and the quantized output can be analyzed.
CDF plotting and Figure 1 reproduction.

Code has been implemented that computes and plots the empirical cumulative distribution function Φ of S - rowfill(m) for each format on a linear x-axis spanning roughly [-16, 0], reproducing the layout and axes of Figure 1a.

Code has been implemented that computes and plots the empirical CDF Φ of 2^(S - rowfill(m)) for each format on a log-scale x-axis spanning roughly [10^-6, 10^0], reproducing the layout and axes of Figure 1b.
Quantitative characterization of the five distributions in Figure 1.

In Figure 1a, the CDF of S - rowfill(m) under E4M3 (input format with larger mantissa) most closely tracks the FP32 baseline across the plotted range, while E5M2 shows a visibly coarser/step-like staircase, confirming E4M3's advantage for representing the subtraction result S - rowfill(m).

In Figure 1b, the CDF of 2^(S - rowfill(m)) under pure E4M3 deviates from FP32 in the small-value region [0, 2^-9) due to insufficient resolution, whereas E5M2 tracks FP32 more closely in that region, confirming the claim in Section 3.1 about the exponentiation output range.

In Figure 1b, the mixed-format E4M3xE5M2 CDF (E4M3 input to the exp2 operation, E5M2 output) most closely approximates the FP32 reference distribution among the FP8 configurations, verifying the motivation for a mixed-format strategy stated in Section 3.1.

In both Figure 1a and 1b, the HiF8 CDF closely tracks the FP32 baseline (comparable to or better than the best pure FP8 configuration), supporting the choice of HiF8 as a practical alternative to the E4M3xE5M2 mixed scheme.
The comparison of relative accumulated multiplicative error with vs. without integer-exponent ceiling across sequence lengths reproduces the trend in Figure 2.

Code exists to simulate the accumulated multiplicative error of the online-softmax rescaling factor 2^(m^(j-1) - m^(j)) over a sequence of tiles, computing the relative error against an FP32 ground-truth accumulator.
Code implements the 'without ceiling' variant that updates m^(j) using the raw (non-integer) rowmax of S^(j) and computes powers-of-two with fractional exponents in low precision.
Code implements the 'with ceiling' variant that updates m^(j) using ceil(rowmax(S^(j))) so that all rescaling exponents (m^(j-1) - m^(j)) are integers, making the powers of two exact.
The experiment sweeps sequence lengths spanning at least the range 100 to 500 (matching the x-axis of Figure 2) and records the relative accumulated error at each length for both variants.
Code produces a plot analogous to Figure 2 with two curves (w/o ceiling and w/ ceiling) of relative error versus sequence length.
The 'w/ ceiling' relative error remains tightly bounded and near zero across all tested sequence lengths (matching the flat curve of Figure 2, within a small tolerance of the paper's ~0 magnitude).

The 'w/o ceiling' relative error grows in magnitude with sequence length and reaches an absolute magnitude on the order of ~0.004-0.006 by sequence length 500, reproducing the drift shown in Figure 2.
At every tested sequence length, the absolute relative error of the 'w/ ceiling' variant is strictly smaller than that of the 'w/o ceiling' variant, confirming the ordering shown in Figure 2.
